Exercise II: Mark the statements true / false

(1) The car ran out of gas about two miles from here. False

(2) She was too frightened to tell the details of the incident. False

(3) The Girl went to the police to report the matter. False

(4) Second Man wanted to save himself from the storm. True

(5) First Man wanted to go to town for business. True

(6) They heard the hum of a motor in the distance. True

(7) She could not remember the description of the killer. True

(8) She bolted the door before the man came near. True

Exercise III: Answer the following questions

(a) Why couldn't the Girl describe the killer?

The Girl could not describe the killer because she was too frightened and she had seen him only in flashes of lightning. She saw the woman's hand, head and long light hair being dragged in the mud, but she does not remember the man's face at all, nor whether he was wearing a hat. Fear had wiped out every detail of his appearance.

(b) What were the circumstances that forced her to leave her car?

The Girl had been at a party and thought she had enough gas to get home, eight miles away. About a mile from the bus station her car ran out of gas. There were very few cars at that hour of the morning, so she locked her car, took her flashlight and started walking down the road, hoping to catch the bus and return for the car later.

(c) Why did she ask for help from First Man?

She asked First Man for help because he was the only person in the bus station, and she was terrified and being chased by the killer. She rushed in sobbing, bolted the door and cried, "Thank God! You're here!" She believed that a fellow human being in the station would protect her from the man outside.

(d) What was the condition of the weather?

The weather was stormy. Heavy rain was falling, lightning flashed again and again, and large bursts of thunder followed. The storm was so severe that the bus was late, the light in the station dimmed with every flash, and no one could travel safely on the road.

(e) How did Second Man accuse First Man of lying?

Second Man accused First Man of lying because, when he looked in through the glass door, he had seen somebody else in the room. First Man had tried to suggest that there was no one else there. Second Man said plainly, "You tried to tell me there was no one else here. What was the idea of lying?"

(f) Does the Girl become suspicious of First Man as the play progresses?

At first the Girl trusts First Man completely as her helper and protector. She does not suspect him at all while he comforts her and questions her. Her trust turns to horror only at the very end, when he takes out a flashlight from his coat pocket — her own flashlight, which she had dropped while running from the killer. Then she realizes that he himself is the killer.

(g) What is her impression about Second Man?

At first the Girl is terrified of Second Man, because his face pressed against the glass in a flash of lightning seems to be the killer's face. Then she finds him rough and forward: he grabs her arm, insists that she should go with him, and laughs at her fear. In the end she realizes that he was not the killer at all, only a traveller who wanted shelter from the storm.

(h) Why didn't she accompany Second Man?

She did not accompany Second Man because his manner frightened her and she trusted First Man more. Second Man grabbed her arm and said, "We'll have it all to ourselves," which alarmed her. She refused firmly, saying, "No — No — I won't. Leave me alone. I'm going to stay here — with him."

Exercise IV: Answer the following questions in 100-150 words

(a) Write down the story of the play in your own words.

On a stormy night a young Girl of about twenty-three rushes into a lonely bus station on a deserted highway. Her car has run out of gas, and while walking she saw a man dragging a woman's corpse out of a car in the lightning. She fled through the woods and reached the station, where a pleasant Man of about thirty-five comforts her and advises her to go to the police, though she cannot describe the killer. A Second Man then forces his way in from the storm, and the Girl fears he is the killer. But the Second Man is only a traveller, and he leaves laughing. When the Girl and the First Man are alone again, the Man takes out a flashlight — the Girl's own flashlight, which she dropped while running. She realizes with horror that he is the killer. She bolts the door, and a dog that has come in from the storm jumps and seizes the Man with its sharp teeth, forcing him to run away. The Girl is saved.

(b) Have you had any experience of a similar situation? Write at least ten sentences.

No, I have never faced a situation as frightening as the Girl's, and I hope I never do. Once, however, I was caught in a heavy storm on my way home from school, and for a few minutes I felt something of her fear. The rain was pouring, the lightning flashed, and the road was almost empty. I ran to the nearest shop and waited there until the storm passed. The shopkeeper comforted me and gave me a glass of water, just as the First Man comforted the Girl. That day I learned how important it is to stay calm in danger and to seek help from people nearby. I also learned that one should never travel alone late at night on a deserted road. If I ever saw a crime, I would at once inform the police, because it is our duty. The play teaches us that presence of mind and courage can save a person even in great danger.

(c) Why did the Girl consider First Man her helper?

The Girl considered First Man her helper because he was the only person in the station when she rushed in, terrified and pursued. He caught her as she almost fell, calmed her, gave her a seat, and listened to her story with sympathy. He protected her by hiding her in the Women's room when the Second Man rattled the door, and he refused to go away with the Second Man. He advised her to go to the police and assured her that she would be safe. His gentle, fatherly manner made her trust him completely. She had no reason to suspect that the kind man comforting her was the very killer she was running from, and that is the tragic irony of the play.

(d) What are the factors that played a role in saving the Girl?

Several factors played a role in saving the Girl. First, she outran the killer and lost him by circling round and round in the woods, so that she reached the bus station alive. Second, the bolted door of the station kept the killer out for a time. Third, she refused to accompany the Second Man, whose rough manner frightened her, and chose to stay where she felt safer. Fourth, her own memory returned at the crucial moment: when the First Man produced her flashlight, she recognized him as the killer and bolted the door before he could reach her. Finally, a dog that had come into the station to save itself from the storm jumped and seized the Man with its sharp teeth, forcing him to run away. Thus her courage, her quick action and a lucky chance together saved her life.

(e) How did she realize the truth?

She realized the truth when the First Man took out a flashlight from his coat pocket. It was her own flashlight, which she had dropped on the road while running away from the killer. Only the killer could have picked it up where she dropped it. The Man had been questioning her again and again about what she had seen, and now his possession of her flashlight proved that he was the man by the car. In horror she cried out, ran to the Centre door and bolted it before he could come near her. Then the dog attacked him, and she was saved. The flashlight, a small everyday object, became the clue that exposed the murderer.

(1) She sobs and rushes to the Man quickly. (to, down, along, of, over, in, with)

Key Points

  • A one-act thriller: on a stormy night a young Girl flees a killer and takes shelter in a lonely bus station.
  • The First Man comforts her and seems her helper — but his own flashlight, dropped by the Girl, proves that he himself is the killer.
  • The Girl is saved by her courage, the bolted door and a dog that seizes the killer.
  • Theme: appearances deceive — fear can blind us, and the real danger may stand beside us.

Exercise 2: Mark the statements true or false

(i) Ellen is going to marry John, a farm boy. True

(ii) A girl should prefer to marry a hardworking and ambitious boy. True

(iii) The space man looked like a monster. False

(iv) Kreton cannot read the minds of the people. False

(viii) Kreton gives his consent to spend the night. True

(ix) General Powers thinks that Kreton is a spy. True

(x) The race of Kreton is violent like the human race. False

Exercise 3: Answer the following questions

(i) How does Kreton prove his extraordinary powers? Write five sentences.

Kreton proves his extraordinary powers in several ways. First, he hears what is inside people's minds: he tells General Powers exactly what he is thinking, that he dreams of three silver stars on his shoulder instead of two, that is, of his promotion. Second, he speaks all the languages of the Earth. Third, his spaceship has no instruments, no food and nothing inside, yet it travels between dimensions. Fourth, he puts an invisible wall around his ship, so that the soldiers cannot get near it. Fifth, when Powers and his AIDE rush at him, they stop stunned within a foot of him, because no one can touch him.

(ii) What is the purpose of Kreton's visit?

The purpose of Kreton's visit is simply a visit to our small planet. He has been studying the Earth for years as a hobby, especially this period of its development, when human civilization is only in its initial stages. In the end he reveals a further purpose: he has come to take charge of the whole world, because he believes people will be much happier under his rule.

(iii) How much advanced is the civilization of Kreton than that of the Earth?

The civilization of Kreton is far more advanced than that of the Earth. His people started visiting the Earth long before there were people on this planet. They travel casually between dimensions, they do not die, they control their thoughts, and they see everything through special monitors without travelling. By contrast, human civilization is only in its initial stages: Kreton says that men would need another five hundred years even to understand his explanation of space travel, and about two thousand years to understand time.

(iv) Can the people of the Earth compete with those of Kreton?

No, the people of the Earth cannot compete with those of Kreton. Human power — troops, martial law, weapons and suspicion — is helpless against him. General Powers surrounds the house with soldiers and declares martial law, yet he cannot touch Kreton, cannot enter his ship, and cannot stop him from reading his mind. Kreton's people have conquered death itself, while men are, in his words, poor fragile butterflies with brief little moments in the sun. The two civilizations are not on the same level at all.

(v) How damaging is violence in life? Write five sentences.

Violence is very damaging in life. First, it breeds fear and hatred between people and nations, and destroys peace of mind. Second, it wastes the wealth of nations on armies, weapons and martial law instead of schools, health and progress. Third, it corrupts judgment: General Powers suspects every stranger of being a spy sent before an invasion. Fourth, it destroys innocent things, like Mrs. Spelding's rose garden and the peace of a happy home. Fifth, it keeps humanity in a primitive stage, because a violent race cannot rise to the higher civilization that Kreton's people have reached.

(vi) What type of life do you foresee in the year 5000?

In the year 5000, I foresee a life free from hatred and violence, as the theme of the play suggests. Men will have conquered disease and perhaps even death, and will travel easily between the planets. There will be no armies and no martial law, because nations will have learned to live in peace. People will feel pride in the service of humanity rather than in power over others. Science will have explained time and space, and human beings will control their thoughts and emotions as Kreton's people do. Life will be happier, longer and nobler than it is today.

(vii) How impressive were the morals of Kreton?

The morals of Kreton are very impressive. He is gentle, honest, humorous and peace-loving: he never dreams of invading the Earth, and he assures General Powers that none of his people would dream of it. He loves human beings as a hobby and approves of everything they do, even their primitive ways. He is kind to the Spelding family and polite to everyone. At the same time he is playful and a little arrogant in his superiority, and his final announcement that he will take charge of the world shows that even a highly moral being can be tempted by power.

(viii) What is the role of General Powers in the play?

General Powers plays the role of the military mind and of human suspicion. He surrounds the Spelding house with troops, declares martial law, cuts off the telephone, and interrogates Kreton for two hours, because his job is to guard the security of the country. He suspects Kreton of being a spy sent before an invasion, and he wants to take the spaceship apart for military use. His complete failure — he cannot touch Kreton or enter the ship — proves that human military power is helpless before a superior civilization. He is also a comic figure, dreaming of his promotion to three stars.

(ix) What is the theme of Kreton's study?

The theme of Kreton's study is the Earth and its people in their present, primitive stage of development. He has studied the planet for years, especially this period when human civilization is only beginning. He is fascinated by the rawness of human emotions, by the fact that men do not control their thoughts, and by their violence, suspicion and pride. He studies them as a hobby, the way a human being might study an interesting but backward tribe. His study leads him to the conclusion that human beings are still children in the story of civilization.

(x) How does Kreton impress General Powers?

Kreton impresses General Powers by powers that no soldier can match. He tells Powers his secret thought — that he dreams of three silver stars, that is, of his promotion — and Powers is startled to find him correct. He shows a spaceship with no instruments that still travels between dimensions. He puts an invisible wall around the ship, so that the soldiers cannot approach it. Finally, when Powers orders his AIDE to grab Kreton, both men stop stunned within a foot of him, because no one can touch him. Powers, who began by calling him a monster and a spy, ends helpless and amazed.

Exercise 4: Answer the following questions in 100-150 words

(i) Write a note on: (a) Mr. Spelding (b) Mrs. Spelding (c) Ellen (d) John (e) General Powers (f) Kreton.

(a) Mr. Spelding (Roger Spelding) is a middle-aged TV newscaster, known as 'Father America', unctuous and resonant in manner. He is proud, self-important and fond of his broadcasts, and he dreams of being the first journalist to interview Kreton. As a father he wants Ellen to marry a hard-working, ambitious man who will make his mark, not a farm boy. (b) Mrs. Spelding is his bored, vague wife, who knits passively and worries most about her rose garden, which the spaceship has damaged. She finds Kreton comforting, like Grandfather Spelding, because of his whiskers. (c) Ellen, a lively girl of twenty, is engaged to John. She is kind, curious and fascinated by Kreton, and she hopes he will stay with the family. (d) John Randolph is Ellen's fiance, a farm boy who grows English walnuts on his own farm. He is brave — he runs toward the landing spaceship — and simple and honest. (e) General Powers is a vigorous National Guard general, obsessed with security, who declares martial law and suspects Kreton of spying. (f) Kreton is a mild, pleasant man in his forties, dressed in the fashion of 1860, with side-whiskers. He reads minds, speaks all languages, never dies, and ends by announcing that he will take charge of the whole world.

(ii) How does the playwright expose the inferiority of the present race to that of the future?

The playwright exposes the inferiority of the present race through a constant contrast between Kreton and the human beings. Kreton's people travel between dimensions, read minds, speak all languages, put invisible walls around their ships, and do not die; human beings need troops, martial law, telephones and weapons, and all of these fail. Kreton tells them plainly that they are only in the initial stages of civilization, that they would need five hundred years to understand his explanation and two thousand years to understand time. Human suspicion is shown as primitive: Powers at once thinks of spies and invasion, while Kreton's people have never dreamed of invading anyone. Even human pride is childish beside Kreton's calm superiority. The play thus makes the audience feel how backward, violent and fearful the present race still is, and how far it has to travel toward the peaceful, rational civilization of the future.

(iii) Describe the arrival of the flying saucer in your own words.

On a starry night a luminous object arcs slowly across the sky and comes down toward the Spelding house in Silver Glen, Maryland. John rushes in shouting that it is coming this way and will land right there. The family watches from the house as the shining object, not much larger than a car, lands right in Mrs. Spelding's rose garden. Its whole side opens, and a man steps out — mild and pleasant looking, in his forties, with side-whiskers and dressed in the fashion of 1860. John shakes hands with him and brings him up to the house. Meanwhile Mr. Spelding telephones General Powers, who arrives with troops, surrounds the house and declares martial law. The visitor introduces himself as Kreton, from another planet in another dimension, come simply to visit this small planet which he has studied for years as a hobby.

(iv) Compare and contrast the people of the two planets.

The people of Kreton's planet and the people of the Earth are sharply different. Kreton's people are peaceful: they have never dreamed of invading anyone, they do not trade, and they do not die. They travel between dimensions, read minds, speak all languages, and see everything through monitors without travelling. They control their thoughts, while human thoughts run wild with raw, uncontrolled emotions. Earth people, by contrast, are violent and suspicious: they keep armies, declare martial law, suspect every stranger of spying, and fight over things they do not have. They are short-lived — poor fragile butterflies, as Kreton calls them — and their civilization is only in its initial stages. Yet both peoples share curiosity, pride and love of family: the Speldings are warm and hospitable, and Kreton himself loves human beings as a hobby. The difference is not in worth but in age: one race is grown up, the other is still a child.

(v) Write a story of your visit to a far off place in the north of Pakistan.

Last summer I visited Hunza, a far-off valley in the north of Pakistan, and the journey itself was an adventure. We travelled by bus along the Karakoram Highway, past deep ravines, roaring rivers and snow-capped peaks, until we reached Karimabad, the main town of Hunza. The valley was green and peaceful, with apricot orchards, poplar trees and old forts — Baltit Fort and Altit Fort — standing on the hillsides. The people were kind and hospitable; they offered us dried apricots and butter tea, and the children showed us the way to the Attabad Lake, whose blue water shines between the mountains. We visited the Passu Cones, the white peaks that look like a row of sharp teeth, and we watched the sunset over Rakaposhi. At night the sky was full of stars, clearer than I had ever seen. I returned home with the feeling that the north of Pakistan is one of the most beautiful places on Earth, and that its people, like the Speldings, are simple, brave and warm-hearted.

Key Points

  • Kreton, a visitor from another planet in another dimension, lands his spaceship in Mrs. Spelding's rose garden.
  • He reads minds, speaks all languages, never dies and travels between dimensions — far beyond human science.
  • General Powers answers with troops and martial law, but human power cannot touch Kreton.
  • Theme: human civilization is still in its initial stages — violent, fearful and suspicious beside a peaceful, rational race.

lessons.title: Play 3: The Oyster and the Pearl (William Saroyan)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise I: Write short answers to these questions

(1) Where does the play take place?

The play takes place in Harry Van Dusen's barber shop in O.K.-by-the-Sea, California, a small town with a population of 909. The sea is a block down the street, and the shop is crowded with odds and ends washed up by the sea.

(2) Why is Harry sitting in the barber's chair?

Harry is sitting in the barber's chair because Clay Larrabee, a boy of nine or ten, is giving him a haircut. Harry and Clay exchange haircuts free of charge: Harry gives Clay a haircut free, and Clay gives Harry one free. That is why, at the opening of the play, the barber himself is in the chair.

(3) According to Harry, how does one bring merriment to the tired old human heart?

According to Harry, one brings merriment to the tired old human heart by composing a symphony, painting a picture, writing a book, or inventing a philosophy. He tells Clay that such a person may be the one man hidden away in the junk of the world who brings joy to tired hearts.

(4) What is Harry's philosophy?

Harry's philosophy is the 'Take-it-easy' way — a way to live. It means relaxing, taking one's time, enjoying the sea, fishing, reading and laughter, instead of hurrying and worrying. Harry admits that the trouble with his philosophy was that he kept forgetting to take it easy, until he came to O.K.-by-the-Sea and found the proper place to stop.

(5) How much did Harry pay for his barber shop? How long has he been in O.K.-by-the-Sea?

Harry paid seventy-five dollars for his barber shop. He had eighty dollars to his name, and the old barber sold him the shop for seventy-five and threw in the haircut. He has been in O.K.-by-the-Sea for twenty-four years.

(6) How many barbers are there in O.K.-by-the-Sea?

There is only one barber in O.K.-by-the-Sea, and that is Harry Van Dusen himself. He says plainly, 'Nobody would [get a haircut], since I'm the only barber.'

(7) How much does Harry charge for a haircut?

The regular price of a haircut is a dollar, but Harry says it is too much for a haircut, so he generally takes a half or a quarter. He adds, 'Now and then I do. Now and then I don't,' because most of the people of the town are too poor to pay even that.

(8) Where is Clay going?

Clay is going down to the beach to look for stuff washed up by the sea. He says, 'This time I'm going to find something real good, I think.'

(9) Why does Clay need money?

Clay needs money for two reasons: he wants to get his father to come home again, and he wants to buy his mother a present. The family is living off the money they saved from the summer they worked, and there is not much left.

(10) What has happened to Clay's father?

Clay's father, Clark Larrabee, picked up and went off the day after Clay's last haircut, about a month ago. All he said was 'Enough's enough,' which he wrote on the kitchen wall. The family thought he would be back in a day or two, but he did not return, and now they have to find him and bring him back.

(11) What does Clay want to put in the local newspaper?

Clay wants to put an advertisement in the local newspaper, The O.K.-by-the-Sea Gull, which comes out every Saturday. The ad says: 'Clark Larrabee. Come home. Your fishing tackle's in the closet safe and sound. The fishing's good, plenty of cabazon, perch, and bass. Let bygones be bygones. We miss you. Mama, Clay, Roxanna, Rufus, Clara.'

(12) Who is Miss McCutcheon? How does she feel about her job?

Miss McCutcheon (Vivian McCutcheon) is the new teacher at the school in O.K.-by-the-Sea, in town since last Sunday. One week at the school has knocked her for a loop: she wants to quit and go home to San Francisco, yet at the same time she has a feeling she ought to stay. She asks Harry's advice: 'Shall I go, or shall I stay?'

(13) What is Miss McCutcheon looking for? How does she feel about the children of the town?

Miss McCutcheon is looking for a chance to teach — not for a husband, as Harry teases her; she expects a husband to look for her. About the children she feels despair: they do not care about anything, whether they get good grades or bad, whether they pass or fail, or anything else. Almost all of them are unruly, and the only things they seem interested in are games and the sea. Nobody seems to have any sensible ambition; it is all fun and play. That is why she is on her way to the beach on a Saturday, to watch them and understand them better.

(14) What does Harry advise her to do?

Harry advises her to go back to San Francisco while the going's good. He says, 'You're too good for a town like this. Too young and too intelligent.' He means that a clever, serious young teacher will only be disappointed in a town where nobody cares for learning.

(15) What kind of haircut does Miss McCutcheon want?

Miss McCutcheon wants a poodle haircut.

(16) Can Harry give a poodle haircut?

No, Harry cannot give a poodle haircut. He does not know how to give one, and even if he knew how, he would not do it. He does not give women haircuts at all: the only women who visit his shop bring their small children for haircuts. He tells her, 'In my sleep, in a nightmare, I would not cut your hair.'

(17) What does Miss McCutcheon think that a poodle haircut will do for her appearance?

Miss McCutcheon thinks that a poodle haircut will make her look more plain and simple, so that she fits into the scenery around her. She has decided to stay, and she believes that changing her appearance — and dressing differently too — will make the children take her seriously, instead of thinking her nothing more than a pretty girl who is going to give up and go home in despair.

(18) Where has Clark Larrabee been? How did he get to O.K.-by-the-Sea?

Clark Larrabee has been working in Salinas. He got to O.K.-by-the-Sea by getting a ride down in a truck, which is now across the street at the gasoline station. He is only passing through, hoping to run into Clay, and he has not been home at all: he has left his wife Fay.

(19) What does Clark give Harry? For what purpose?

Clark gives Harry three ten-dollar bills — thirty dollars — and asks him not to tell Clay who gave the money. The purpose is that Clay should take the money home to his mother. It is the first money Clark has been able to save, and he hopes that when he makes some more, he will send it to Harry to hand to Clay to take home.

(20) How far is it to Hollywood from O.K.-by-the-Sea?

It is about two hundred miles straight down the highway from O.K.-by-the-Sea to Hollywood. Harry tells the writer, 'About two hundred straight down the highway. You can't miss it.'

(21) What work does the Man do?

The Man is a writer. He writes 'a little bit of everything.' He is on his way to Hollywood, and he has stopped in O.K.-by-the-Sea while they change the oil in his car across the street, to get a haircut and get it out of the way.

(22) What did Clay find near Black Rock?

Near Black Rock, Clay found an oyster. The tide hardly ever gets low enough for a fellow to get around to the ocean side of Black Rock, but a little while ago it did, so Clay went around there, poked about, and found the oyster. He did not happen to find it; he went looking for it.

(23) What does Clay believe is in the oyster? How much is it worth?

Clay believes that there is a big pearl in the oyster. The oyster is shut tight and alive, and Clay says the pearl in it is worth at least three hundred dollars.

(24) Does Miss McCutcheon believe that there is a pearl in the oyster?

No, Miss McCutcheon does not believe that there is a pearl in the oyster. She says the truth is that there is no pearl in it: only one oyster in a million has a pearl, so truth favors the probability that this is not the millionth oyster. She wants to open the oyster and show the children that there is no pearl in it, so that Clay will begin to face reality.

(25) Why does Miss McCutcheon have a chair with three legs?

Miss McCutcheon is carrying a cane chair without one leg and without a seat, which she picked up at the beach. That is why it has only three legs. Like everybody else in the town — the children, Judge Applegarth, Fenton Lockhart and Harry himself — she has begun bringing things home from the sea.

(26) What kind of judge is Judge Applegarth?

Judge Applegarth is not a real judge at all. He judged animals — hounds, or dogs — at a county fair one time, so the town calls him Judge. Nobody ever checked up on it; he said he did it, and that certainly entitled him to be called Judge Applegarth.

(27) What year is it?

It is 1953. When Miss McCutcheon asks, 'Are we living in the Middle Ages, Mr. Van Dusen?' Greeley answers, 'No, this is 1953, Miss McCutcheon.'

(28) What does Greeley have in a bottle?

Greeley has sea water in a bottle. He insists that there are little living things in the water, which cannot be seen now but will show up later, because the water of the sea is full of things.

(29) Who suggests that they should open the oyster?

Miss McCutcheon suggests that they should open the oyster. She says to Harry, 'Mr. Van Dusen, shall we open the oyster and show Clay and his sister Roxanna and their friend Greeley that there is no pearl in it?'

(30) Why do they want Wozzeck to come?

They want Wozzeck to come because Harry would rather have Wozzeck open the oyster than open it himself: 'I'd rather he opened this oyster. I might damage the pearl.' Wozzeck repairs watches, radios and alarm clocks and sells jewelry, so he is the expert for the job. Secretly, Harry also plans that Wozzeck, who has a few pretty good-sized cultivated pearls, will pretend to find a pearl in the oyster, so that Clay gets his three hundred dollars.

(31) How does Harry describe the inhabitants of O.K.-by-the-Sea?

Harry describes the inhabitants of O.K.-by-the-Sea as all poor. Most of them cannot afford to pay for the haircuts he gives them. A few find jobs for a couple of months every year, North or South, come back half dead of homesickness, and live on next to nothing the rest of the year. A few get pensions. Every family has a garden and a few chickens, and they make a few dollars selling vegetables and eggs. In a town of almost a thousand people there is not one rich man, not even one who is well off. 'And yet,' Harry says, 'these people are the richest I have ever known.'

(32) How does Miss McCutcheon view Harry's thinking about the pearl in the oyster?

At first Miss McCutcheon strongly opposes Harry's thinking: she calls it a trick and his 'mumbo-jumbo ideas,' and asks whether he plans to put pearls in oysters for every poor child in the world. But in the end she gives in and asks what he wants her to do. She agrees to be just a little less sure about things when she talks to the troubled children, and to let Clay come around to the truth easily enough as soon as he gets his father home.

(33) Why does the Judge think that Miss McCutcheon will not last as a teacher? What kind of teacher does he think is needed?

The Judge thinks Miss McCutcheon will not last a month because she is too pretty. He says, 'Too pretty. Our school needs an old battleaxe like the teachers we had when we went to school.' By an old battleaxe he means a strict, experienced teacher who establishes strong discipline — the opposite of a young, pretty newcomer like Miss McCutcheon.

(34) What is Applegarth's complaint about the sea?

Applegarth's complaint about the sea is that the beach is not what it used to be. He does not mind the competition he is getting from the children; his complaint is that the quality of the stuff the sea is washing up is not good any more. As a beach comber, he finds that there is nothing worth picking up and taking home.

(35) What kind of gadget does the writer describe?

The writer describes a gadget in New York, like a safety razor, with which anybody can give anybody else a haircut. There was a full-page advertisement about it in last Sunday's Times, and it costs two dollars and ninety-five cents. A father could save a lot of money giving his children haircuts with it, though the writer admits it is a question of effectiveness, because a boy is ashamed of a bad haircut.

(36) Who buys the oyster? How much does he pay?

The writer buys the oyster. He offers Clay three hundred dollars for it, and hands Clay the money. Clay asks Harry if it is all right, Harry looks at the writer, who nods, and Harry says, 'Sure it's all right.'

(37) Does the writer open the oyster? Why not?

No, the writer does not open the oyster. When Wozzeck asks if he wants to open it first, he says, 'No, I want the whole thing. I don't think the pearl's stopped growing.' He wants to keep the oyster whole, with the dream intact, rather than risk finding nothing inside.

(38) Why does Clark Larrabee return?

Clark Larrabee returns because he saw the classified advertisement in The Gull. He and his truck were ten miles up the highway when he happened to see the ad: 'Clark Larrabee. Come home... We miss you.' So he came back to the house after all, for the weekend, and he says that in two or three months he thinks he will have enough to come back for a long time. He is taking Clay fishing the next morning.

(39) What does the writer do with the oyster?

The writer holds the oyster in front of him as if it were an egg, looks at it carefully, turning it in his fingers, and then puts it in his coat pocket and takes it away unopened. He does not open it at all. As he says, 'As far as I'm concerned, the whole thing's a pearl.'

Exercise II: Questions for discussion

(1) Do you think that it is right to allow Clay to believe that there is a pearl in the oyster? Explain briefly.

Yes, I think it is right, as Harry argues. Clay does not really want money; he wants his father to come home, and the belief in the pearl keeps him going while the family waits. Truth can come gently later, when his father is home and he is no longer troubled. To crush his dream at once, as Miss McCutcheon first wants, would only hurt a child who has already lost his father for a month. On the other hand, Miss McCutcheon's view also has force: truth is supposed to set us free, not imprison us. Harry's answer is a middle way — be a little less sure about things with troubled children, and let the truth come in its own time.

(2) In your opinion, why is the writer willing to buy the pearl? What has he received in return? What does he mean by saying: 'As far as I'm concerned, the whole thing's a pearl.'

The writer is willing to buy the oyster because he sees in it something more valuable than a pearl: a boy's faith, a poor family's hope, and a whole story worth telling. In return he has received the oyster itself, unopened, and the experience of O.K.-by-the-Sea — material for his writing and a glimpse of human goodness. By saying 'the whole thing's a pearl' he means that the oyster, with Clay's dream still alive inside it, is itself precious. Opening it might destroy the dream, but keeping it whole preserves the wonder, and that wonder is the real pearl.

(3) What has attracted Harry and other people to O.K.-by-the-Sea? Is it the kind of town that appeals to you? Do you think that it resembles an ideal town? Give reasons for your answer.

Harry and the other people are attracted to O.K.-by-the-Sea by the sea and the hills, and above all by the chance to take one's time — to live without hurry, worry and competition. Harry stopped there twenty-four years ago because he decided he was not looking for anything anymore, and he found a place where he could take it easy. The town appeals to me for its kindness, its leisure and its closeness to nature, but it also has real faults: everybody is poor, there are few jobs, and ambitious young people like Miss McCutcheon find nothing to do. It resembles an ideal town only in its human warmth and its freedom from hurry; as a place to live and work, it is far from ideal, because an ideal town must also offer opportunity and a future.

(4) Harry's philosophy is of 'Take it easy' (Relax and enjoy life) nature. How does that philosophy appeal to you? Why or why not? Do you think that this philosophy works better in small towns than in large cities? Explain.

Harry's 'Take it easy' philosophy appeals to me because modern life is full of hurry, worry and competition, and everyone needs rest, laughter and time for family and nature. Relaxing and enjoying life is not laziness; it is what keeps a person healthy and human. But the philosophy cannot be followed blindly: a person must also work, study and meet his responsibilities, or he will fall behind. I think it works better in small towns than in large cities, because in a small town like O.K.-by-the-Sea needs are few, neighbours know one another, and life moves slowly. In a large city, rents, jobs and crowds force people to hurry, and taking it too easy can mean losing one's livelihood.

(5) In your opinion, does the play reveal the author's view of life? If so, what is his view of life?

Yes, the play clearly reveals Saroyan's view of life. As the book's own Theme section says, the play is a sentimental comedy which demonstrates faith in the basic goodness of human nature. Saroyan finds people eminently fascinating and wonderful, although a little 'odd' at times. His view is that life should be enjoyed, relaxed and 'played' as the play progresses, rather than hurried through; that poor, ordinary people are often the richest in spirit; and that kindness, hope and dreams matter more than money or strict facts. Even the oyster teaches this: the dream inside it is worth more than any pearl that could be found by opening it.

(6) Would you call this play one of 'The action plays'? Why or why not? How would you describe the play to a friend?

No, I would not call this play one of 'the action plays.' There is almost no action in it: nobody fights, nobody chases anybody, and there is no strong plot and no hero. People simply come into a barber's shop, talk, tell stories and go out again. I would describe it to a friend as a gentle, humorous and heart-warming comedy about a small seaside town — a play of characters rather than events, in which a poor boy's dream of a pearl in an oyster brings his father home and teaches a young teacher to be less sure of herself. It is a play to enjoy and relax with, not a thriller.

(7) Do you think that this would be a good play to produce? Why or why not?

Yes, I think this would be a very good play to produce. It needs only one simple set — a barber's shop — and a small cast of ordinary people, so it is cheap and easy to stage. Its humour is gentle, its ending is happy, and its message about human goodness appeals to every audience. The parts are enjoyable to act, especially Harry, Miss McCutcheon and the Judge. The only difficulty is that the play has little action, so the actors must hold the audience by their talking and their characters alone. A good cast could do that easily, and the play would leave the audience smiling.

Exercise III: WHO SAID IT?

(a) 'At the same time I have a feeling I ought to stay.' Identify the speaker; to whom, on what occasion, and something about the speaker.

The speaker is Miss McCutcheon (Vivian McCutcheon), the new teacher at the school in O.K.-by-the-Sea. She says it to Harry Van Dusen in his barber shop, when she is asking his advice whether she should quit after one week and go home to San Francisco, or stay. She is a pretty young girl with long blonde hair, who carries a colorful parasol. She is serious about teaching — she is looking for a chance to teach — but the unruly children, who care only for games and the sea, have knocked her for a loop.

(b) 'There's no excuse for this town at all, but the sea is here and so are the hills.' Identify the speaker; to whom, on what occasion, and something about the speaker.

The speaker is Harry Van Dusen, the barber of O.K.-by-the-Sea. He says it to Miss McCutcheon in his shop, when he is describing the town and its people to her. The people are all poor, most cannot afford his haircuts, and there is not one rich man in a town of almost a thousand — yet the sea and the hills are there, and that is enough to keep him. Harry is the only barber in town, a man of about sixty who has been there twenty-four years, who wears a different hat every day and lives by his 'Take-it-easy' philosophy.

(c) '....Clay....well, a fellow like that, you can't just go off and leave him.' Identify the speaker; to whom, on what occasion, and something about the speaker.

The speaker is Clark Larrabee, Clay's father. He says it to Harry Van Dusen in the barber shop, near the end of the play, after he has come home for the weekend because he saw the advertisement in The Gull. He means that a boy like Clay — brave, hopeful, believing in his pearl — cannot simply be abandoned. Clark is a working man who left his wife Fay after one too many fights about money, worked in Salinas, and now realizes that he must return to his family. He is taking Clay fishing the next morning.

(d) 'It's shut tight, it's alive, and there's a pearl in it, worth at least three hundred dollars.' Identify the speaker; to whom, on what occasion, and something about the speaker.

The speaker is Clay Larrabee, a boy of nine or ten. He says it to Harry Van Dusen in the barber shop, when he brings in the oyster he found near Black Rock. Clay is a poor boy whose father has left home; he needs money to bring his father back and to buy his mother a present. He is hopeful and determined: he went looking for the oyster deliberately, and he firmly believes that a big pearl is inside it.

(e) 'It's never too soon for any of us to face the truth, which is supposed to set us free, not imprison us.' Identify the speaker; to whom, on what occasion, and something about the speaker.

The speaker is Miss McCutcheon, the new school teacher. She says it to the children — Clay, Roxanna and Greeley — in Harry's shop, when she is arguing that the oyster should be opened to show them there is no pearl in it. She believes in facing facts early: truth, she says, is supposed to set us free, not imprison us. She is young, pretty, serious and idealistic, and she has yet to learn Harry's gentler wisdom about troubled children.

(f) 'Our school needs an old battleaxe, like the teachers we had when we went to school.' Identify the speaker; to whom, on what occasion, and something about the speaker.

The speaker is Judge Applegarth (Arthur Applegarth), the beach comber of O.K.-by-the-Sea. He says it to Harry Van Dusen in the shop, after Miss McCutcheon has gone out, when he declares that she won't last a month because she is too pretty. By an 'old battleaxe' he means a strict, experienced teacher who keeps strong discipline, like the teachers of his own school days. The Judge is not a real judge: he once judged hounds at a county fair, and the town has called him Judge ever since.

Exercise IV: OPTIONAL ACTIVITY

(1) Write a composition of 100-150 words explaining why you liked, or did not like, this play.

I liked this play very much, because it is gentle, humorous and full of human kindness. Unlike most plays, it has no villain and no violent action; its charm lies in its characters — Harry with his 'Take-it-easy' philosophy, Clay with his brave belief in the pearl, Miss McCutcheon learning to be less sure of herself, and the Judge with his beach-combing wisdom. The story is simple but moving: a poor boy's dream brings his father home, and a writer pays three hundred dollars not for a pearl but for the dream itself. The play teaches that hope and goodness matter more than facts and money, and it leaves the reader smiling. I also liked the seaside setting and the easy, natural dialogue. If I did not like anything, it is only that the play has so little action that a restless reader might find it slow. But for anyone who enjoys character and humour, it is a delightful play.

(2) Write a composition describing your ideal town.

My ideal town would be a small, clean town by the sea or in the green hills, like O.K.-by-the-Sea but with more opportunity. It would have good schools with kind, patient teachers, a small hospital, a library and a park where children can play safely. The people would know one another, help one another in trouble, and live without hurry or noise. There would be work for everyone — fishing, farming, small crafts and a few offices — so that no father would have to leave his family to find a job far away. The streets would be safe at night, the air would be fresh, and the town would have a playground, a sports ground and a hall for concerts and dramas. Above all, my ideal town would combine the warmth and leisure of O.K.-by-the-Sea with the chances of a modern town, so that young people could both dream and achieve.

Key Points

  • Harry Van Dusen keeps a barber's shop in O.K.-by-the-Sea and lives by his 'Take-it-easy' philosophy.
  • Clay, a poor boy, believes a big pearl worth three hundred dollars lies in the oyster he found near Black Rock.
  • The writer buys the oyster unopened for three hundred dollars — the dream inside it is the real pearl — and Clay's father comes home.
  • Theme: faith, hope and human goodness matter more than money or cold facts.

Exercise 2: Mark the statements true or false

(i) The poet hears leaves drinking rain. True

(ii) The rain drops make the leaves rich. True

(iii) The green leaves drinking water create a noise. True

(iv) The sunshine darkens the round drops of rain. False

(v) The sunshine, after the rain, makes the scene lovely. True

Exercise 3: Add two more rhyming words in each line

(i) leave, ________, ________

(ii) drop, ________, ________

(iii) rain, ________, ________

rain, again, main (also: plain, train).

Exercise 4: Write a critical appreciation of the poem

Write a critical appreciation of the poem 'The Rain'.

W.H. Davies' short poem 'The Rain' is a musical picture of a shower and its aftermath. The poet hears the leaves drinking rain: the rich leaves on top receive the drops first and pass them drop by drop to the poor leaves beneath, making a sweet noise. The poem has a symbolic meaning too: as the book's Theme explains, the rich at the upper level get the golden chance first, and whatever remains trickles down to the people at the level beneath. When the rain stops and the sun comes out, a wondrous light fills each dark, round drop, and the poet hopes the sun will shine bright and make a lovely sight. The diction is simple and musical, the rhymes (rain/again, top/drop, near/hear) fall gently on the ear, and the whole poem shows Davies' favourite themes — nature and the hardships of the poor — in two short stanzas.

Exercise 5: How can a rainy day be enjoyed?

How can a rainy day be enjoyed?

A rainy day can be enjoyed in many ways. One can sit by a window and watch the rain falling on the leaves, listening to its sweet music, as the poet does. Children enjoy splashing in puddles, making paper boats and floating them in running water, and getting wet in a warm shower. At home, a rainy day is a good time for reading a book, drinking hot tea, eating pakoras, and playing indoor games with family. Farmers welcome the rain because it waters their crops. In short, a rainy day becomes enjoyable when we accept it cheerfully instead of complaining about it, and find pleasure in nature's music, in play, and in the company of family.

Exercise 6: Explain the first stanza with reference to context

Explain the first stanza of 'The Rain' with reference to context.

Reference: These lines are taken from the poem 'The Rain' by W.H. Davies. Context: The poet is describing a shower of rain on the leaves of a tree, and the sweet sound it makes. Explanation: The poet says that he hears the leaves drinking rain. The rich leaves on the top of the tree, which are full of water, give drop after drop to the poor leaves beneath them. It is a sweet noise to hear — these green leaves drinking near. The stanza has a symbolic meaning as well: the rich at the upper level receive Nature's gifts first, and only what remains trickles down to the poor below. The poet's simple, musical words make the scene of the rain come alive before our eyes.

Key Points

  • The poet hears the leaves drinking rain — the rich leaves on top pass drops to the poor leaves beneath, making a sweet noise.
  • After the rain stops, the sun comes out and fills each dark, round drop with wondrous light.
  • Symbolic meaning: the rich get Nature's gifts first; only what remains trickles down to the poor.
  • Theme: nature's music, and the hardships of the poor.

Exercise 4: Explain the first stanza with reference to context

Explain the first stanza of 'Loveliest of Trees, the Cherry Now' with reference to context.

Reference: These lines are taken from the poem 'Loveliest of Trees, the Cherry Now' by A.E. Housman. Context: The poet is describing the cherry tree in full bloom in spring, standing along a path in the woodland. Explanation: The poet says that the cherry, the loveliest of trees, is now hung with bloom along its boughs. It stands beside the woodland ride, wearing white for Eastertide — that is, its white blossoms look like a white dress worn for the Easter festival. The stanza shows the poet's deep love of nature: the cherry in bloom is so beautiful that it seems to dress itself in white for a celebration.

Exercise 5: What time of the year is mentioned in the first stanza?

What time of the year is mentioned in the first stanza?

Eastertide is mentioned in the first stanza — that is, the spring season around Easter, when the cherry tree is in full bloom and wears its white blossoms like a white dress.

Exercise 6: Read the second stanza carefully and write how old is the poet?

Read the second stanza carefully and write how old is the poet?

The poet is twenty years old. He says that out of his three score years and ten — that is, seventy years, the expected span of life — twenty years will not come again, because they are already past. Taking twenty from seventy leaves him fifty more springs to enjoy. So the poet, at the time of writing, is twenty years of age.

Exercise 7: What is the poet trying to say in the last stanza of the poem?

What is the poet trying to say in the last stanza of the poem?

In the last stanza the poet is trying to say that life is too short to enjoy the beauty of nature fully. Since even fifty springs are little room — too short a time — to look at things in bloom, he will not waste any chance: he will go about the woodland to see the cherry hung with snow. The message is that we should seize every opportunity to enjoy the beauty around us, because life passes quickly and its pleasures will not return.

Key Points

  • The cherry is loveliest in spring, hung with bloom and wearing white for Eastertide.
  • The poet is twenty; of his threescore years and ten, twenty will not come again, leaving fifty springs.
  • Life is short — even fifty springs are little room to look at things in bloom.
  • Theme: seize every chance to enjoy the beauty of nature, for life passes quickly.

lessons.title: Poem 4: O Where are You Going? (W.H. Auden)
lessons.notes_html:
Exercise 1: Summarize the poem in your own words

Summarize the poem 'O Where are You Going?' in your own words.

The poem is a dialogue between two imaginary persons personified as reader and rider. The rider is a bold and courageous person, ambitious to make his way through thick and thin toward the pass of glory. The reader, full of awe and reverence, warns him that the valley beyond is full of dangers: the furnaces burn, the midden's bad smell sickens and maddens the mind, and the gap is the grave where the tall return. Then fearer speaks to farer, and horror speaks to hearer, trying to discourage the traveller with doubts — that dusk will delay him, that his footsteps will fail from granite to grass, that a bird in the twisted trees and a spot on his skin mean disease and death. But the rider is not stopped: he leaves them there, saying 'Out of this house' and 'Yours never will,' and goes on his way. The poem teaches that the way to glory and success is vague and uncertain, but it can be paved through with courage and perseverance.

Exercise 2: Answer the following questions

(i) What kinds of feelings does the poet create in the minds of his readers?

The poet creates feelings of awe, fear, suspense and curiosity in the minds of his readers. The warnings of the reader, the fearer and the horror fill the reader with dread about the dangers ahead — burning furnaces, maddening smells, graves, dusk, disease and death. At the same time the rider's boldness creates admiration and hope. The mixture of fear and courage keeps the reader in suspense until the end, when the rider leaves his discouragers behind.

(i) How do you feel after reading the poem?

After reading the poem I feel both afraid and encouraged. The warnings about the valley, the grave and the disease are frightening, and they make me realize how many dangers lie on the road to success. But the rider's courage encourages me: he does not listen to fear, and he goes on his way. I feel that fear is only a voice trying to stop us, and that a brave person must leave it behind and keep moving toward his goal.

(ii) What does the title of the poem signify?

The title 'O Where are You Going?' signifies the question that fear and doubt put to every ambitious person. The reader asks the rider where he is going, because his journey seems dangerous and foolish. The question stands for all the warnings of the world: where are you going, and do you know the dangers ahead? The poem answers that a courageous person knows his goal and goes on, even when others question his journey.

(iii) Write down the rhyming words in the poem.

The rhyming words in the poem are: burn — return (first stanza); pass — grass (second stanza); trees — disease (third stanza); and reader — farer — horror — there (last stanza). The opening words of the first three stanzas — rider, farer, hearer — also echo one another in sound.

(iv) Explain the third stanza of the poem in your own words.

In the third stanza horror speaks to hearer. Horror asks, 'O what was that bird?' and asks whether the hearer saw a shape in the twisted trees. Horror warns that behind him, swiftly and softly, a figure is coming, and that the spot on his skin is a shocking disease. In other words, horror tries to frighten the traveller with mysterious shapes, unseen followers and signs of illness, so that he will give up his journey. The stanza shows how fear invents dangers — a bird, a shape, a spot — to discourage a brave person.

(b) That dusk will not delay on your path to the pass. False

(c) Your footsteps feel from granite to grass. True

(d) The spot on your skin is a shocking disease. True

Key Points

  • A dialogue between a bold rider and a fearful reader who warns him of the dangers ahead.
  • The valley holds burning furnaces, a grave, disease and dusk — yet the rider goes on toward the pass.
  • Fear speaks in many voices — reader, fearer, horror — but courage leaves them behind.
  • Theme: ambition must face fear and doubt on the road to glory.

Exercise 5: Write a critical note on the poem

Write a critical note on the poem 'In the Street of the Fruit Stalls'.

Jan Stallworthy's poem is a symbolic picture of life in a poor street at evening. In the dark street, lit only by lanterns, fruit sellers pile melon, guava and mandarin in pyramids that glow red-hot and gold-hot from within, like cannon balls. Dark children with a coin to spend enter the lantern's orbit, buy fruit, break it open, and let its gold or silver fountain wet their mouths, fingers, cheeks, noses and chins. Radiant as lanterns, they forget the dark street the poet is standing in. The poem's power lies in its contrast: the world is threatened with war, misery and poverty, yet these have failed to crush man's love for pleasure. The children's joy, innocent and complete, shines against the darkness. The imagery is vivid and sensuous — colour, light, taste and touch all combine — and the short, musical lines make the scene glow like the lanterns themselves.

Exercise 6: Give a summary of the poem in your own words

Give a summary of the poem 'In the Street of the Fruit Stalls' in your own words.

It is evening in a dark street of fruit stalls. The lantern wicks balance their flames, and a dark dew falls. Melon, guava and mandarin are piled in pyramids like cannon balls, glowing red-hot and gold-hot from within in the lantern light. Dark children, each with a coin to spend, come into the circle of lantern light and look at the fruit: the moon is compacted to a rind, the sun is in a pitted skin. They buy a fruit, break it open, and let its gold or silver juice wet their mouths, fingers, cheeks, noses and chins. Radiant as lanterns themselves, they forget the dark street in which the poet stands watching them. The poem thus shows how a small pleasure can make poor children forget their misery for a while.

Exercise 7: What are the feelings of the poet standing in the dark?

What are the feelings of the poet standing in the dark?

The poet, standing in the dark street, feels both pity and wonder. He pities the poor children and the misery of the world around them — the darkness, the war and the poverty that threaten life. At the same time he feels wonder and delight at the children's innocent joy: radiant as lanterns, they forget their misery in the sweet spray of the juice. His feelings are therefore mixed — sadness for the dark world, and admiration for the human love of pleasure that even poverty cannot crush.

Exercise 8: Why has the poet used 'cannon balls' to describe the fruit?

Why has the poet used 'cannon balls' to describe the fruit?

The poet has used 'cannon balls' to describe the fruit for two reasons. First, the shape: the melons, guavas and mandarins are piled in pyramids, round and heavy like cannon balls stacked for a gun. Second, the contrast: cannon balls are instruments of war and destruction, while fruit is a symbol of life and pleasure. By calling the fruit cannon balls, the poet reminds us that this is a world threatened by war — yet the fruit, glowing red-hot and gold-hot, turns the weapons of war into objects of joy. The image thus joins the poem's two themes: war and pleasure.

Exercise 9: Paraphrase the last stanza in your own words

Paraphrase the last stanza of the poem in your own words.

The children take the fruit, break it open, and let its golden or silver juice flow over their mouths, fingers, cheeks, noses and chins. Shining as brightly as the lanterns themselves, they completely forget the dark street in which the poet is standing. In other words, the children's delight in the fruit is so complete that it makes them forget their poor and dark surroundings for a time.

Exercise 10: Make a list of fruits described in the poem

Make a list of fruits described in the poem.

The fruits described in the poem are: melon, guava and mandarin. The melon is like the moon compacted to a rind, and the mandarin (small orange) is like the sun in a pitted skin. All three are piled in pyramids like cannon balls and glow red-hot and gold-hot from within in the lantern light.

Key Points

  • On a dark evening street, lantern light makes piles of melon, guava and mandarin glow like cannon balls.
  • Dark children with a coin each buy fruit, break it open and let its gold or silver juice wet their faces.
  • Radiant as lanterns, they forget the dark street — small pleasure defeats war and poverty for a while.
  • Theme: the love of pleasure survives even in a world threatened by war and misery.

Exercise 3: Give a summary of the poem in your own words

Give a summary of the poem 'A Sindhi Woman' in your own words.

A Sindhi woman walks barefoot through a bazaar, carrying a stone jar high on her head. She moves with the same undulant grace as the cloth blown back from her face, gliding smoothly with not a ripple in her tread. The poet watches her cross erect over the stones, garbage, excrement and crumbs of glass in the Karachi slums. He himself, with his stoop — bent by an idle, unburdened life — reflects that they stand most straight who learn to walk beneath a weight. The poem is thus a tribute to a working woman, who has practically turned her work into an art, walking softly with the delicacy and rhythm of a dancer's feet.

He realized that only those who bear the burden of life and carry its hardships through life are strong and straight, while an idle person, who carries no weight, soon decays and stoops.

What is the main idea of the poem 'A Sindhi Woman'?

The main idea of the poem is that work creates rhythm in life and keeps a person strong and vigilant, while idleness makes a person decay. It is a tribute to a working woman: the Sindhi woman, carrying a stone jar through the Karachi slums, has practically turned her work into an art. There is a time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to pluck up that which is planted; a time to break down and a time to build up; a time to weep and a time to dance. In other words, nothing in this world happens out of place: birth and death, sowing and harvesting, destruction and construction all come at their own appointed times, and man must accept this divine schedule with patience.

Exercise 4: Write in your own words the critical appreciation of the poem

Write in your own words the critical appreciation of the poem 'Times'.

The poem 'Times', taken from Ecclesiastes (3:1-12), is a solemn meditation on the order of life. Its theme is that everything happens at an appropriate time: there is a time when winter sets in and a time when winter is gone and another season sets in; nobody is born before time, nor dies before time; there is a time to sow seeds and a time when their fruits are ripe to be plucked. Nothing in this world happens out of place; everything is scheduled according to a specific time. The poem's power lies in its parallel structure — 'a time to...' repeated again and again — which gives it the rhythm of a sermon and the dignity of scripture. Its language is simple, yet its message is profound: man should accept the seasons of his life, in joy and in sorrow, with patience and faith.

  • A time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to pluck up; a time to weep and a time to laugh.
  • Nothing happens out of place — birth, death, sowing and harvest all come at their appointed times.
  • Theme: life runs on God's schedule; man must accept the time appointed for each thing.

Exercise 5: Give a summary of the poem

Give a summary of the poem 'Ozymandias'.

The poet met a traveller from an ancient land who told him that in the desert stand two vast, trunkless legs of stone. Near them, half sunk in the sand, lies a shattered face — a visage with a frown, a wrinkled lip and a sneer of cold command. The sculptor understood the king's passions well, and stamped them on the lifeless stone; the hand that mocked them and the heart that fed them are both gone. On the pedestal of the statue are inscribed the proud words: 'My name is Ozymandias, king of kings: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' But nothing beside remains. Round the decay of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare, the lone and level sands stretch far away. The poem is thus an ironic picture of human pride destroyed by time.

Exercise 6: What kinds of feelings does the poem create in the reader's mind?

What kinds of feelings does the poem create in the reader's mind?

The poem creates feelings of irony, pity and awe in the reader's mind. Irony, because the proud boast on the pedestal — 'Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' — is mocked by the empty desert around it, where nothing remains. Pity, because the great king who thought he had toppled the world is now only a broken statue in the sand. Awe, because the poem makes us feel the power of time, which brings all the luxuries of life to an end and levels kings and common men alike. It also creates humility: the reader feels that all feelings of superiority in man are only an illusion and self-deception.

Exercise 7: What did the traveller see in the desert?

What did the traveller see in the desert?

Near them, on the sand, half sunk, lay a shattered visage — the broken face of the statue — with a frown, a wrinkled lip and a sneer of cold command. On the pedestal of the statue he read the words: 'My name is Ozymandias, king of kings: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' Around the colossal wreck there was nothing else — only the lone and level sands stretching far away.

Key Points

  • A traveller in the desert finds two vast, trunkless legs of stone and a shattered face half sunk in the sand.

  • The sculptor stamped the king's pride on the lifeless stone; the hand that mocked and the heart that fed are gone.
  • Theme: human pride and power are destroyed by time.

Exercise 5: Explain the last three lines of this poem with reference to the context

Explain the last three lines of 'The Feed' with reference to the context.

Reference: These lines are taken from the poem 'The Feed' by Ahmed Nadeem Qasmi. Context: The mother sparrow has brought only one grain of millet for her ten tiny young ones, and the poet turns to the reader with a question. Explanation: The poet says that man has learnt to set life on foot — that is, human beings have learnt great skills, like splitting the atom and starting new life. Then he asks, 'Could you split the grain?' — could man, with all his science, divide one tiny grain of millet fairly among ten hungry young ones? The last line repeats the problem: 'One grain to be fed to the ten young ones.' Exercise 6: Write a critical appreciation of the poem

Write a critical appreciation of the poem 'The Feed'.

Ahmed Nadeem Qasmi's poem 'The Feed' is a very simple poem with a deep meaning. It describes a mother sparrow who brings a single grain of millet in her beak to feed her ten young ones, who are so tiny and small that from head to toe they are beaks when they cry. The poet then turns the picture into a question for mankind: man has learnt to split the atom and to set life on foot, but could he split one grain among ten hungry mouths? The poem's beauty lies in this contrast between the smallness of the scene and the greatness of its message — a mother's love, the problem of poverty and sharing, and the limits of human science. The language is plain and touching, the image of the ten open beaks is unforgettable, and the closing question stays in the reader's mind long after the poem ends.

What do you feel after reading the poem 'The Feed'?

I feel admiration for the mother sparrow's love and devotion, which makes her bring whatever she can find to her nest. I also feel thoughtful: the poet's question — could man, who can split the atom, split one grain among ten? — makes me realize that science cannot solve every human problem, and that love and sharing matter more than power.

Key Points

  • A mother sparrow brings a single grain of millet in her beak to feed her ten tiny young ones.

  • Man can split the atom, but can he split one grain among ten hungry mouths?
  • Theme: a mother's love, and the limits of human science before God's creation.

Exercise 5: Write a critical note on the poem

Write a critical note on the poem 'The Hollow Men'.

T.S. Eliot's 'The Hollow Men' is a powerful modern poem about the emptiness of modern life. The poet calls modern men 'hollow men' and 'stuffed men': they lean together, their heads are filled with straw, and their dried voices, when they whisper together, are quiet and meaningless as wind in dry grass or rats' feet over broken glass in a dry cellar. They have shape without form, shade without colour, paralysed force and gesture without motion. The poem's imagery is strange and haunting — straw-filled heads, dry cellars, broken glass — and its short, broken lines sound like the meaningless whispering they describe. Its message is that human beings have become soulless: they depend on each other but cannot make a society, and they only seem to be walking souls, while actually they are not even that.

Exercise 6: Give a summary of the poem
